title: In the image (Genesis 1:26–27)
hook: every person is made in God's image; the rabbis say a king's coins look alike, but God's people never do (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5)

segments.voice: Yesterday: six days of making, rooms first, then what fills them. Your line was count the good. Did you get to six? Day twenty-four.
screen: `SIX DAYS OF MAKING — COUNT THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Take a coin out of your pocket, or picture one. There's a face on it, a president or a queen. Now take out another coin of the same kind. Same face. Exactly the same, down to the last line of the hair. That's the whole point of a coin: every one stamped from the same die, identical, interchangeable. You don't care which quarter you get. Now look around at the next ten people you see today. Not one of them is the same. Two thousand years ago, the rabbis looked at those two facts side by side, and made them into one of the boldest teachings in Jewish law. Today: the image.
screen: `TWO COINS, THE SAME FACE.` → `TEN PEOPLE, NO TWO ALIKE.` → `THE RABBIS PUT THEM TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: On the sixth day, the Torah slows down. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them." In Hebrew: tzelem Elohim. Tzelem is an image, a likeness, the word used for a statue or a figure. Elohim is God. Every human being, the verse says, carries God's likeness. What that likeness is, the Torah doesn't explain. Maimonides said it's the mind, the ability to understand. Others say it's freedom, the power to choose, or the power to create, or to love. The text leaves the question open. Now the coins. The Mishnah, describing how judges warned witnesses in a capital case, says this. A human king stamps many coins with one seal, and they all look alike. But the King of kings stamped every person with the seal of the first human, and not one of them is like another. God's image makes us different, not the same. And from there the Mishnah goes further. Why was humanity created from a single person? So that whoever destroys one life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life is as if they saved a whole world. And so no one can say to anyone else, my ancestor was greater than yours. And so each person is obliged to say: the world was created for my sake. Two rabbis once argued over the greatest principle in the Torah. Rabbi Akiva said: love your neighbor as yourself. Ben Azzai pointed to the verse about humanity made in God's likeness, and said his was greater, because it covers everyone.
screen: `TZELEM ELOHIM — THE IMAGE OF GOD.` · `WHAT IS THE IMAGE? IT DOESN'T SAY.` · `ONE SEAL, NO TWO ALIKE.` · `ONE LIFE IS A WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `IN THE IMAGE OF GOD CREATED HE HIM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Bring to mind the face of someone you passed today and barely noticed: a cashier, a driver, someone on the street. Try to see them clearly. The shape of the face. The expression. The one detail that makes it theirs and nobody else's. If you believe what the verse says, hold that face as carrying God's image. If you don't, hold it as one entire world. The bell holds the time.
Tzelem Elohim. The image of God, stamped on every person, so that no two are alike.
Your line: no two faces alike. Today, look at one stranger's face with care, long enough to remember one thing that is only theirs. Day twenty-four.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching and law draw on tzelem Elohim for the dignity of every person, from the care of the sick to the honor given to the dead; the Mishnah's saying about saving one life as saving a whole world is widely quoted.

fork.setup: the Mishnah asks: why was humanity created from just one person? which answer does it give?
options: so the world would fill slowly.
so that one life counts as a whole world.
so there would be one family name.
fork.reveal: whoever destroys one life destroys a world; whoever saves one saves a world. and no one can say their ancestor was greater.

original.note: Hebrew: the image of God. tzelem is the word for a likeness or figure.

trapdoor: what you thought: people look like God.
what it means: every person carries God's likeness, and that likeness makes each one different, and each one a whole world.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 turns the coin image into law for witnesses; Maimonides (Guide 1:1) reads the image as intellect; Ben Azzai calls Genesis 5:1 the Torah's great principle.
